newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss farmers unhappy with mad cow cull plan.
newsitem.headline: Swiss farmers unhappy with mad cow cull plan.

text.p: Swiss farmers criticised parliament on Tuesday for approving a scaled-down cull of cows that falls far short of the government's original plan to eradicate "mad cow" disease by slaughtering 230,000 animals.
The bill that won final approval in the upper house on Tuesday calls for wiping out only around 2,300 cows, or one percent of the original total.

"This was the absolute minimum in our view," Farmers' Association spokesman Lorenz Boesch said of the watered-down scheme, adding the group would rather have seen the cabinet's more costly but more comprehensive proposal adopted.
"This had problems primarily for financial reasons, but also emotionally the solution was very controversial. What emerged was what was politically possible," he said.

But Switzerland's mightiest farmers' group believes the last chapter has yet to be written in the story, he said. "We think this is not over yet. Further measures could be needed depending on what happens in the next few months," he said.
The new scheme affects animals from herds where the disease has been reported and which were born before December 1990, the year when Switzerland adopted measures to stem the illness.
In addition, herds that include any cows born after 1990 that contract the disease in future would be culled completely.
The vote was carried by the National Council, the lower house of parliament, on Monday night.

After Britain, Switzerland has the most cases of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE). It has reported 230 cases of the disease. Scientists suspect tainted beef products can trigger the brain-wasting Creuzfeldt-Jakob Disease in humans.

The coalition government proposed in September that 230,000 cows should be slaughtered to eradicate the disease in Switzerland once and for all. That programme would have cost around 320 million Swiss francs.
Farmers would also have had to contribute to the plan through lower milk prices and would have got 1,000 francs per cow slaughtered.
The new scheme will cost only around eight million francs and pay farmers 3,500 francs per slaughtered cow.
Their skulls and backbone marrow will be burned, but their meat can be sterilised at high heat, processed into animal meal and fed to pigs and chickens, the Federal Veterinary Office said.
The plan sets aside another 25 million francs to reduce the oversupply on markets by buying some 10,000 to 15,000 cows. Boesch said they would be burned if no other use could be found.

In 1990 Switzerland banned feeding cows with beef bone and remains which could help spread the disease. It also recommended the slaughter of direct offspring of BSE-infected cows to help boost consumer confidence.
But some countries have banned beef imports from Switzerland and the Swiss themselves are eating less beef.
Switzerland said last month it would limit beef imports from Europe from January 1 for health reasons.
New rules will require imports of beef products be guaranteed free of internal organs and nerve tissue, which are considered most likely to spread mad cow disease.
